I've been farming these 30.4 mu in Quzhou for 30 years now. I'm 48, didn't go past primary school, but I learn from my own fields and from watching my neighbors. My household has five people, but some of the younger ones work off-farm in town, so I can't always count on help at home — that means I need to be practical with labor and not try anything too fancy.

For the winter wheat, I'll plant an improved variety like Jimai22, same as most people in the village. I'll do rotary tillage before sowing in October — the machine service comes around and it's quick and cheap. For fertilizer, I'll put about 22 kg of nitrogen per mu. I've tried going lower than 20, but the yield drops too much and I lose money. Going much above 25 kg is just throwing cash away. I don't bother much with phosphorus or potassium — the soil here seems okay for those, and adding more doesn't make much difference in my experience. I'll irrigate three times using my well: once before winter to help the seedlings survive, once at jointing in spring, and once when the heads come out. I'll spray pesticides three times for weeds and pests.

For the summer maize, there's no time for tillage after wheat harvest — sometimes we only have three or four days before we need to get the seeds in the ground — so I plant with no-tillage. Everyone here uses hybrid corn, mostly Denghai605. I'll apply about 15 kg nitrogen per mu, less than wheat because the soil still has something left from the wheat season and I need to watch my costs. I'll irrigate twice, once when the seedlings need it and once at the big trumpet stage. Three pesticide sprays should be enough to keep the weeds and borers under control. I expect about 520 kg per mu for wheat and 560 kg per mu for maize — that's what I usually get when the water is good and I don't cut corners too much.
